Vera Rubin · Native LUT-B · Accuracy first

Can Vera Rubin run accurate 3-bit LLM inference?

We study one question: can Rubin's native LUT-B instruction run 3-bit model weights and 3-bit KV cache without destroying model quality?

Answer: yes—but only with the right quantizer. Calibrated non-uniform codebooks and scales keep the quality loss bounded. A naive 3-bit codebook can increase perplexity by thousands of times. The algorithm, not the bit width alone, decides whether INT3 works.

Rubin LUT-B and our algorithm

What the kernel does

A native decompress::lut::b MMA multiplies an E4M3 A tile by a compressed B tile. Each B element is stored as a 3-bit index. The index selects one of eight E4M3 reconstruction values held in Tensor Memory. Lookup and multiplication happen inside the tensor-core instruction, so the kernel does not first materialize a dense BF16 or FP16 B matrix.

This primitive supports two useful LLM paths:

  • W3A8 weights: A is an online-quantized activation and B is a model weight (W^\top) packed offline.
  • K3V3 cache: A is Q or P, while B is packed Kᵀ or V. FP32 softmax remains between the two LUT-B matrix multiplications.

How the kernel computes the product

The mathematical operation remains (Y=A\cdot B), but B is reconstructed only inside each MMA:

B̂[k,n] = global × scaleB[t,n] × LUT[t][index[k,n]]
Y[m,n] = Σₜ Dₜ[m,n] × scaleA[m,t] × scaleB[t,n] × global
  1. Tile the GEMM. One 128-thread CTA owns an M128×N8 output tile and walks K in 64-element segments. Activations are quantized per row/K block to E4M3 plus a UE8M0 scale.
  2. Stage the payload. The 3-bit indices are rearranged into the 256-byte shared-memory image expected by the instruction. The eight-value LUT and A fragment are staged in Tensor Memory.
  3. Issue native LUT-B. The kernel executes tcgen05.mma…decompress::lut::b. Hardware looks up B and accumulates an FP32 partial D; an mbarrier prevents reading D before the MMA completes.
  4. Apply scales. The MMA produces the product of the E4M3 A values and LUT-reconstructed E4M3 B values. Before adding that partial to Y, the epilogue restores the original magnitudes by multiplying it by the activation scale and weight scale for the current K segment. A single tensor-global FP32 factor is applied once to recover range that cannot be represented by the tile-local E4M3 codebooks.

The two scale layouts used in the study are:

  • K64 scale: one conceptual UE8M0 byte for each of the eight output rows in a K64×N8 tile. The tile contains 192 B of indices, 8 B of LUT values, and 8 B of scale metadata: 208 B, or 3.25 bit/weight.
  • Two-K32 scale: one scale for each output row and each K32 half. The 16 scale bytes produce a 216 B tile, or 3.375 bit/weight. The correctness harness expands these conceptual one-byte scales to FP32 for epilogue arithmetic; the bit budget counts their intended packed representation.

Direct K32 LUT-B is illegal on this instruction, so two-K32 is implemented with two full-K64 MMAs:

  1. Pass 0 zeros the upper 32 A columns and computes only the lower K32 contribution.
  2. Pass 1 zeros the lower 32 A columns and computes only the upper K32 contribution.
  3. Each partial is multiplied by its own A and B half-scale before the two results are added.

This is algebraically exact for the two-K32 quantization contract: the masked half contributes zero, while the active half receives the correct local scale.

What makes this kernel difficult

Speed challenges

  • B-only decompression constrains scheduling. Q×Kᵀ and P×V are legal, but optimized attention schedules that place long K/V in A cannot use LUT-B directly.
  • The M tile has 128 rows. Batch-1 decode may supply only four GQA rows; one routed expert may receive only a few tokens. Without request batching or expert gathering, most rows are padding.
  • Software scale application breaks the K pipeline. The correctness kernel reads every FP32 partial from Tensor Memory before applying tile-specific scales. It therefore cannot keep one accumulator resident across the full K loop.
  • Two-K32 issues two MMAs. It often improves accuracy, but it doubles MMA issue count and costs about 10% wall clock in the current end-to-end native evaluation.
  • The current MiniMax path uses launch blocking. This removes overlap between launches and is intentionally a correctness contract, not a production schedule.

Accuracy and correctness challenges

  • Three bits provide only eight reconstruction values. Uniform levels waste resolution on outliers; the codebook must be fitted to the actual tensor distribution.
  • Scale granularity changes the quantizer. A scale that is too coarse clips large values; excessively local scales increase metadata and may require another kernel pass.
  • A is also quantized. W3A8/K3V3 quality includes E4M3 activation, Q, and P rounding, not only 3-bit B error. Softmax max, exponentiation, sum, and normalization therefore stay FP32.
  • Runtime transforms must match offline transforms. H64-rotated weights require the same signed H64 transform on A; AWQ and OSCAR need their inverse or absorbed transforms in the correct locations.
  • TMEM synchronization is part of numerical correctness. Reading an accumulator before MMA completion can produce intermittent non-finite tiles even if the payload itself is correct.

How we make 3-bit LUT-B work

The offline quantizer chooses the eight values, the index of every element, and the scale layout. The runtime then uses the same payload in one of two ways:

  • Weight use: pack static (W^\top) once; quantize each activation row to E4M3 online; optionally apply H64 to A; execute one LUT-B GEMM for each linear layer or routed expert.
  • KV use: keep sensitive sink/recent tokens in BF16; seal older Kᵀ and V into LUT-B payloads once; execute Q×Kᵀ, FP32 softmax, then P×V at every decode step.
  1. Condition. Optionally rotate or rescale the tensor to reduce outliers.
  2. Fit. Learn eight E4M3 reconstruction values for each tile offline.
  3. Correct. For weights we compare RMS², Fisher/SqueezeLLM, GPTQ, H64, AWQ, and inter-GPTQ. For KV we compare uniform, Lloyd–Max, and OSCAR codebooks.
  4. Pack. Store 3-bit indices, the 8-value LUT, and UE8M0 scales.
  5. Execute. Rubin looks up B inside the MMA; A remains E4M3.

TurboQuant is a related learned-centroid KV baseline, but it is not relabelled as a Figure 2 result because its available measurements use a different runtime and evaluation protocol.

Experiment 1 — 3-bit weights

We compare 18 quantized configurations plus BF16 and A8 baselines across Qwen3-4B, Gemma4-12B, and MiniMax-M3 at 8K, 64K, and 128K. The question is whether algorithm choice can make native W3A8 usable.

What the compared algorithms do

  • Lloyd–Max / uniform / NF3. Uniform spaces eight levels evenly; NF3 uses a fixed normal-inspired codebook; Lloyd–Max learns eight centroids from each tile. This isolates whether fitting the codebook matters.
  • RMS² / SqueezeLLM. RMS² weights reconstruction error by activation second moments. SqueezeLLM instead uses diagonal Fisher information. Both change the codebook fit; neither is GPTQ compensation.
  • GPTQ / inter-GPTQ. GPTQ uses a block Hessian to push each rounding error into columns not yet quantized. Inter-GPTQ alternates this compensation sweep with refitting the eight-value codebook.
  • H64 / AWQ / scale variants. H64 spreads outliers with a signed Hadamard transform and applies the matching transform to A. AWQ rescales activation channels and folds the inverse scale into weights; K64/two-K32/global variants change scale granularity.

Every reported quantized GEMM runs through the native Rubin LUT-B MMA.

Result: 3-bit weights are viable, but a naive codebook can be orders of magnitude worse.

Experiment 2 — 3-bit KV cache

Figure 2 compares five Qwen KV configurations (BF16 plus four compressed recipes) and three Kimi latent-cache configurations. It asks whether a fitted codebook and controlled scales can make native K3V3 accurate while reducing cache traffic.

What the KV algorithms do

  • Window and sealing. Sink and recent tokens remain BF16. Older K/V are sealed once in 64-token chunks as 3-bit indices, layer-specific LUT values, and scales; decode never writes them again.
  • Lloyd–Max codebooks. Each layer learns eight non-uniform values from calibration data, placing resolution where K/V values occur. Uniform levels waste codes on sparse tails and collapse PPL.
  • OSCAR. A calibrated rotation and clipping rule spreads outliers before fitting the codebook. It can improve some models, but adds transforms unless they are absorbed into adjacent projections.
  • Native attention path. E4M3 Q multiplies compressed Kᵀ; max, exp, sum, and normalization stay FP32; E4M3 P then multiplies compressed V. Both cache reads use B-side LUT decompression.

Result: From PPL, 3-bit KV is practical when the codebook and scale are controlled. Uniform INT3 is not a usable baseline.

What speedup could W3A8 and K3V3 enable?

These are kernel roofline estimates, not end-to-end serving measurements. They separate the benefit of moving fewer bytes from the online cost of the more elaborate accuracy methods.

W3A8 weight-GEMM estimate

Native weight path Payload Extra online work Kernel implication
One-pass K64 LUT-B 3.25 bit/W None beyond A8 quantization 2.49–4.35× Rubin BF16; 16.3–28.6× H100 BF16 at 40–70% LUT-B rate
LM / RMS² / GPTQ / SqueezeLLM / inter-GPTQ Same K64 payload Codebook, Fisher, and Hessian work is offline Same one-pass envelope; byte ceilings are 4.92× Rubin and 32.3× H100
H64 + K64 3.25 bit/W Signed H64 transform on A Base envelope minus the transform cost; often buys the largest accuracy gain
Two-K32 scale oracle 3.375 bit/W Two masked K64 MMA passes 2× MMA issue; ≈10% wall-clock premium in the current native evaluation

Folded AWQ and a tensor-global scale add no extra GEMM pass when the fold is supported. The current correctness kernel is not optimized, so this table describes the attainable kernel envelope rather than its present wall clock.

K3V3 attention estimate at 1M context

Qwen3-4B attention path KV / request Attention-only tok/s vs H100 BF16
H100 · BF16 KV 154.6 GB 21.7 1.00×
Rubin · BF16 KV 154.6 GB 142.3 6.57×
Rubin · K3V3, LUT-B rate 40% 30.2 GB 353.7 16.3×
Rubin · K3V3, LUT-B rate 55% 30.2 GB 486.3 22.4×
Rubin · K3V3, LUT-B rate 70% 30.2 GB 619.0 28.6×
Rubin · K3V3 byte ceiling 30.2 GB 727.6 33.6×

Qwen3-4B, 36 layers, GQA4, attention only. The model includes a 320-token BF16 sink/recent window, so the effective 1M cache uses 3.129 bit/value rather than exactly 3.125. These estimates exclude model weights, MLP, sampling, communication, and scheduling. Lloyd–Max is offline; OSCAR adds rotation/clipping unless absorbed into neighbouring projections.

Conclusion 1 — W3A8. Most “fancy” quality methods are offline and preserve the one-pass K64 kernel. H64 pays an A transform; two-K32 pays a second MMA pass.

Conclusion 2 — K3V3. A fitted codebook and controlled scales can cut a 1M KV cache from 154.6 GB to 30.2 GB. Actual speed then depends on LUT-B rate and small-M scheduling, not on another dequantization pass.
